documents.title: Prostate Cancer Treatment

chunks.content: 1 Introduction Prostate cancer (PCa) is the most common non-skin cancer and the leading cause of cancer deaths in 48 countries, and it has been identified as the fifth leading cause of death worldwide [ ]. Age, African-American race, family history, and germline mutations are well-established nonmodifiable risk factors for PCa, and metabolic syndrome, excessive body weight, and smoking have been identified as potential modifiable risk factors [ , ]. The incidence and mortality among black men compared to white men are 1.7 and 2.1 times as high as those among white men, respectively [ ]. The majority of new cases are diagnosed in 65–74 year-old men, and it is a very uncommon cancer in men younger than 45 years old. Autopsy studies show that up to 80% of men will harbor PCa by the age of 80 years old; however, most such cancers are slow-growing, low-grade, relatively harmless, and have little impact on survival in this age group [ ]. The aggressiveness of PCa is highly variable and largely depends on the initial grade at diagnosis. Patients with a Gleason score of 8–10 (Grade Groups 3–5) can progress from localized disease to metastasis and death within a relatively short time period, whereas patients with a Gleason score of 6 (Grade Group 1) may never experience symptoms or disease progression [ ]. PCa can be detected at an early, asymptomatic stage, while it is still curable. This is called screening. Screening for PCa has been primarily based on prostate-specific antigen (PSA), with the objective of detecting PCa in its early stages, thereby reducing PCa-specific mortality [ ]. A recent systematic review showed that the digital rectal examination has a notably low diagnostic value as an independent screening test or supplement to PSA (positive predictive value 21%); however, it is an essential part of clinical work-up of elevated PSA [ ]. Therefore, PSA is the primary screening test for PCa. However, PCa screening remains controversial, with varying recommendations among medical societies and governments [ ]. This controversy arises from concerns about potential overdiagnosis and overtreatment of low-risk PCa, complications from unnecessary biopsies, and the magnitude of benefits derived from early diagnosis and treatment in relation to the potential harm. Surgery and radiation therapy are the main treatment modalities for localized PCa, generally resulting in successful outcomes but carrying the risk of harms, such as erectile dysfunction or urinary incontinence [ , ]. Over the past few years, active surveillance has emerged as an alternative initial management strategy for individuals with PCa of low or low-intermediate risk [ ]. Additionally, several new diagnostic modalities, such as MRI and MRI-targeted biopsy, biomarkers in blood and urine, and tools for individual risk stratification, have entered the clinical landscape of screening and early detection of PCa. This comprehensive review aims to provide the current evidence of PCa screening. The purpose of this review article is to summarize the Level I evidence from randomized controlled trials of PSA screening and treatment for PCa [ ]. 2 Methods A narrative review of randomized controlled trials of PCa screening and treatment was performed. We restricted this review to population-based trials enrolling men at average risk of PCa, i.e. , trials conducted in the general population and not specifically targeting men with specific factors that increase their likelihood of developing PCa compared to the general male population. We retrieved full-text articles of the most recent follow-up publications from the trials based on our extensive expert knowledge of the literature. We did not conduct a formal database search with specific keywords because our familiarity with the key papers in this field allowed us to directly identify the relevant and most up-to-date publications. After data collection, an expert informationist was consulted to conduct a literature search to identify any missed relevant and recent studies, by searching for trials started between 2014 and 2023 using ClinicalTrials.gov, International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP), and International Standard Randomised Controlled Trial Number (ISRCTN). The search confirmed that no recent trials or later publications had been missed. 3 PSA as a screening tool PSA, discovered in 1979 and first used clinically in the late 1980s, has become the primary tool for detecting, staging, and monitoring PCa [ ]. PSA is an enzyme of the serine protease type produced by the columnar epithelium found in the tissue of the prostate. Following its generation within cells, pro-PSA traverses the basal and endothelial cell layers before entering the ducts of the prostate. Once inside, it undergoes a conversion into active PSA, ultimately breaching the capillary membranes to access the systemic circulation. A fraction of this active PSA then experiences proteolysis, transforming into an inactive or “free” PSA upon entry into the bloodstream, where it remains unbound. [ ]. PSA is an enzyme of the serine protease type produced by the columnar epithelium found in the tissue of the prostate. Following its generation within cells, pro-PSA traverses the basal and endothelial cell layers before entering the ducts of the prostate. Once inside, it undergoes a conversion into active PSA, ultimately breaching the capillary membranes to access the systemic circulation. A fraction of this active PSA then experiences proteolysis, transforming into an inactive or “free” PSA upon entry into the bloodstream, where it remains unbound. Active PSA that reaches the bloodstream quickly binds to circulating protease inhibitors. The age-adjusted percentage ratio of free to protein-bound PSA serves as a valuable indicator of PCa, given that the ratio of free PSA to total PSA tends to decrease in cases of malignancy [ ]. Using measurements of concentrations of PSA as a PCa screening tool remains a topic of debate when considering healthy, asymptomatic males. This is due to the fact that elevated serum PSA levels are detected in numerous benign prostatic conditions. Conditions such as benign prostatic hyperplasia, infection, inflammation, or trauma can cause an increase in serum PSA levels, thereby diminishing the specificity of this biomarker as a test to detect PCa [ ]. However, the baseline PSA concentration in midlife has been demonstrated to be a strong prognostic marker of future risk of lethal PCa and can also be used to exclude men at increased risk. For example, men with a PSA level below 1 ng/mL have a very low 25-year risk of developing metastatic PCa or dying from the disease [ ]. Although there is no specific PSA level below which PCa can be ruled out, a PSA level above 3 ng/mL is commonly used to recommend further evaluation ( e.g. , repeating the PSA, performing a digital rectal examination, and considering risk calculators, reflex biomarkers, and/or MRI) before deciding to proceed to a prostate biopsy. 4 Randomized controlled PSA screening trials A summary of the randomized controlled trials of screening and treatment for PCa has been published previously [ ]. In essence, the collective evidence from the screening trials demonstrates that regular PSA screening leads to a reduction in PCa mortality, though the benefits must be weighed against the risks of overdiagnosis and overtreatment. Treatment trials indicate that while prostatectomy and radiation therapy provide excellent outcomes, they are associated with significant risks such as urinary incontinence, erectile dysfunction, and bowel dysfunction [ ]. In detail, four contemporary, high-quality, randomized controlled trials have assessed the effectiveness of a PSA-based screening program on PCa-mortality, representing the available evidence with the most recent follow-up ( ). The multicenter European Randomized Study of Screening for Prostate Cancer (ERSPC) began in the early 90s and enrolled men in nine European countries. The study involved 162 389 men aged 55–69 years old (core age group), and results after a follow-up period of 16 years are currently available [ , ]. The screening group was invited to a blood sample screening protocol every 2–4 years, with a PSA cutoff of 3 ng/mL in most centers to recommend a systematic biopsy, while the control group was not invited to screening (but had some exposure to opportunistic PSA testing in later years of the trial). PCa-specific mortality, the primary outcome, was significantly lower in men who underwent screening compared to the control group: risk ratio (RR) 0.80 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.72–0.89, p <0.001) at 16 years of follow-up. As the absolute benefit and follow-up time increase, the number needed to invite (NNI) and the number needed to diagnose (NND) to prevent one PCa death have been decreasing over time. In the last update at 16 years, the reported values were 570 and 18, respectively [ ], as opposed to the initial follow-up (9 years) values of 1410 and 48, respectively [ ]. Similarly, when the follow-up is extended to 25 years in modeling studies, the NNI and NND decrease to 385 and 11, respectively [ ]. The ERSPC also demonstrates the importance of dynamic, repeated screening. There was a 25% reduction in PCa mortality for those who attended only one screening round, as opposed to a 48% reduction for those who attended at least twice. This difference is explained by the fact that men diagnosed in the first round tended to have incurable disease (prevalence screening), which was much less common in subsequent screening rounds. The 20% reduction in PCa-specific mortality is further substantiated by the Göteborg-1 trial, with an independent study protocol, part of which was included in the ERSPC (the core age group), presenting the longest available follow-up results to date (22 years), and reporting a 77% attendance rate in the screening group (having a PSA-test at least once) [ ]. The 20% reduction in PCa-specific mortality is further substantiated by the Göteborg-1 trial, with an independent study protocol, part of which was included in the ERSPC (the core age group), presenting the longest available follow-up results to date (22 years), and reporting a 77% attendance rate in the screening group (having a PSA-test at least once) [ ]. In this trial, 9950 patients in the screening group were invited to undergo PSA screening every 2 years from age 50 years until 69 years, with a biopsy recommendation if PSA was higher than 3.0 ng/mL initially, and 2.5 ng/mL after 2004. An observed benefit in PCa mortality for the screening group amounted to an approximate 30% reduction (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.55–0.91, p =0.005), with an NNI of 217 and NND of nine. This also represents a decrease from earlier follow-up data (previously 293 and 12, respectively, at 14 years of follow-up) and a larger absolute risk reduction. While a decreasing relative mortality risk reduction was reported over longer follow-up periods (RR 0.71 at 22 years; 0.55 at 14 years), the investigators explained this finding by noting that men in the screening program, on average, stopped screening at 69 years, later constituting a significant portion of PCa deaths in the study group, and there was also increased exposure to opportunistic screening in the control arm. An increased risk of PCa death was reported in men with more than 10 years of follow-up after screening termination, those entering the program after age 60 years, and those who did not undergo testing [ ]. In contrast to these results, the Prostate, Lung, Colorectal, and Ovarian (PLCO) trial, conducted in the United States, initiated in 1993 with the participation of 76 683 men aged 55–74 years, did not show a statistically significant reduction in PCa mortality following a screening protocol compared to usual care. The screening group underwent annual PSA testing and digital rectal examination for 6 years and 4 years, respectively, while the control group received standard practice, which also included PSA testing. The PSA cutoff for recommending a biopsy was set at 4 ng/mL, and follow-up was at the discretion of the men's primary care physicians, with PCa mortality as the primary outcome. The RR for PCa mortality was 0.93 (95% CI 0.81–1.08, p =0.38) at 17 years [ , ]. The main reason that the trial did not detect a difference in PCa mortality between trial arms was the high extent of contamination, i.e. , PSA-testing in the control group, which reduced the statistical power [ ], with 86% of control men undergoing any PSA testing during the trial and nearly half (46%) receiving annual PSA testing (in contrast to approximately 20% contamination in the ERSPC trial). Moreover, the rates of biopsy compliance in men with abnormal PSA levels were 64% in the PLCO experimental group compared to 86% in the ERSPC study. When accounting for contamination in both the ERSPC and PLCO, modeling studies have demonstrated that regular PSA screening in these trials reduced PCa mortality by 30% at 11 years of follow-up [ ]. The impact of a low-intensity PSA screening was assessed in the UK Cluster Randomized Trial of PSA Testing for Prostate Cancer (CAP). A total of 419 582 men were randomized to either a one-time PSA screening test or no screening. A prostate biopsy recommendation was made if PSA levels were ≥3.0 ng/mL. Following a median follow-up of 10 years, no significant difference in PCa mortality was found (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.85–1.08, p =0.50) [ ]. Additionally, a higher number of low-risk PCa cases were identified in the intervention group. However, at 15 years of follow-up, there was a statistically significant reduction in PCa mortality in the intervention group compared to the control group (RR 0.92 [95% CI 0.85–0.99], p =0.03), albeit smaller than other screening trials [ ]. The CAP study has been criticized for using a one-time screening PSA, low adherence to biopsy recommendations, with only 40% of patients in the intervention group complying. Moreover, the use of a single screening round, as established in other studies such as the first round of the Göteborg-1 trial, has been noted to detect more advanced and incurable cancers compared to dynamic screening at regular screening intervals. In addition to these conflicting trial results, PCa screening is associated with potential physical and psychological harms. The transrectal and transperineal biopsy techniques carry a risk of hematuria, hematospermia, dysuria, pain, and infection (5%–7%), which poses a major risk and is the primary cause of hospitalization (1%–5%) [ ]. In addition to these conflicting trial results, PCa screening is associated with potential physical and psychological harms. The transrectal and transperineal biopsy techniques carry a risk of hematuria, hematospermia, dysuria, pain, and infection (5%–7%), which poses a major risk and is the primary cause of hospitalization (1%–5%) [ ]. Those risks, coupled with the psychological distress associated with the biopsy, cancer suspicion, and risk of overdiagnosis, underscore the necessity for engaging in shared decision-making with men before PSA screening [ ]. Nevertheless, once diagnosed with PCa, a man faces the risk of overtreatment of the indolent disease, which can vary between series [ ]. In the USA, the rate of active surveillance for low-risk PCa varies between 4% and 78% depending on many factors including the year of diagnosis (more surveillance in recent years) [ ]. 5 Implementing risk-stratification, biomarkers, and MRI in screening pathways Recent advancements in PCa screening emphasize a risk-adapted strategy using PSA testing alongside factors like age, family history, and PSA density to better stratify risk. Multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) is now recommended before a biopsy to target specific areas and reduce unnecessary procedures. New biomarkers and risk calculators can improve accuracy and minimize false positives. Reflex testing after an initial PSA helps avoid overdiagnosis. Artificial intelligence is being integrated to enhance detection and interpretation. Despite challenges in implementation, these approaches aim for personalized and effective early detection while reducing harms associated with overdiagnosis and overtreatment. The PRAISE-U initiative is a project funded by the European Union to promote a risk-adapted approach to PCa screening across Europe. PRAISE-U aims to implement a more personalized and stratified screening strategy, utilizing tools such as PSA density, risk calculators, and mpMRI, to improve the effectiveness of PCa detection while minimizing unnecessary procedures and overdiagnosis. The initiative also focuses on ensuring appropriate infrastructure, training, and quality assurance to support the integration of these new screening methods into healthcare systems [ ]. MRI has emerged in the past years as an important tool in the diagnostic pathway of PCa and could impact the future screening recommendations. MRI with targeted biopsies to suspicious lesions on MRI has shown potential in the PCa screening and diagnosis pathway. In a recent Cochrane meta-analysis and database review comparing MRI to template biopsies, MRI demonstrated a pooled sensitivity of 0.91 and a pooled specificity of 0.37 for the International Society of Urological Pathology (ISUP) Grade Group ≥2, as well as a pooled sensitivity of 0.95 and a pooled specificity of 0.35 for ISUP grade ≥3. MRI performs best when the PCa diameter is larger than 10 mm [ ]. Additionally, pivotal studies like the PRECISION trial have shown that MRI-targeted biopsies reduce the detection of ISUP Grade Group 1 PCa compared to systematic biopsies (9% vs. 22%, p >0.001) [ ]. These results support the idea of avoiding overdiagnosis and, consequently, overtreating patients by refraining from diagnosing low-risk PCa. Randomized trials have evaluated the implementation of MRI in screening programs ( ). The Stockholm-3 trial was a population-based non-inferiority trial that invited men aged 50–74 years. Those with PSA levels ≥3 ng/mL or a Stockholm-3 test ≥11% (a multiplex test including PSA and other isoforms, clinical and genetic information) were randomly assigned to undergo either a standard biopsy (10–12 cores) or an MRI, along with standard and targeted biopsies in the presence of suspicious lesions. However, only patients with PSA ≥3 ng/mL were included in the final analysis. Within the MRI group, individuals with negative results for clinically significant lesions did not undergo biopsies, except for those with a Stockholm-3 score ≥25%, for whom a standard biopsy was performed. The primary outcome measured was the proportion of clinically significant cancer detected. The results indicated that MRI with targeted and standard biopsies was non-inferior to standard biopsies in detecting clinically significant PCa. In the intention-to-treat analysis, clinically significant cancer was diagnosed in 21% of men in the experimental group and 18% in the control group. Additionally, the percentage of clinically insignificant PCa was lower in the experimental biopsy group compared to the standard biopsy group (4% vs. 12%). The authors reported a 48% lower incidence of patients undergoing biopsies, 73% fewer biopsies with benign findings and 62% fewer clinically significant cancers detected when using an MRI-pathway when normalized to a population of 10 000 men (50–74 years) [ ]. Similarly, the ProScreen randomized trial, conducted in Finland with 61 193 men aged 50–63 years, evaluated the efficacy of a PCa screening protocol involving PSA testing, the 4-kallikrein panel, and MRI. Additionally, the percentage of clinically insignificant PCa was lower in the experimental biopsy group compared to the standard biopsy group (4% vs. 12%). The authors reported a 48% lower incidence of patients undergoing biopsies, 73% fewer biopsies with benign findings and 62% fewer clinically significant cancers detected when using an MRI-pathway when normalized to a population of 10 000 men (50–74 years) [ ]. Similarly, the ProScreen randomized trial, conducted in Finland with 61 193 men aged 50–63 years, evaluated the efficacy of a PCa screening protocol involving PSA testing, the 4-kallikrein panel, and MRI. Among those invited for screening, there was a higher detection of high-grade PCa (1.13%) compared to the control group (0.62%), with an additional one case of high-grade cancer detected per 196 men screened. Low-grade PCa detection was also higher in the invited group (0.26%) compared to the control group (0.14%), with an additional one case of low-grade cancer detected per 909 men screened. These findings are preliminary, and the report of primary PCa mortality outcome of the trial is pending [ ]. The prostate MRI versus PSA screening for PCa detection (the MVP Study), on the other hand, was the first randomized trial to compare PSA testing and prostate MRI for PCa screening. In this study, 525 patients were randomized between MRI and PSA testing. A cut-off of 2.6 ng/mL in the control group and a Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System (PIRADS) 4–5 MRI in the experimental group were established as biopsy recommendations. The MRI protocol resulted in fewer biopsy recommendations (RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.33–0.82, p =0.005), although the total PCa detection, and clinically significant PCa detected, did not reach statistical significance (RR of clinically significant PCa 2.77, 95% CI 0.89–8.59, p =0.07). The study was prematurely terminated due to recruitment challenges during the COVID-19 pandemic, resulting in the study being underpowered [ ]. Moving forward in the effort to reduce the overdiagnosis of low-risk cancer, the Göteborg-2 study investigated whether omitting systematic biopsies for men with an elevated PSA level (≥3 ng/mL) and conducting targeted biopsies of MRI-positive lesions could decrease the risk of detecting clinically insignificant PCa while maintaining the detection of clinically significant PCa. The study took place in a single academic center with double reading of MRI. Men aged 50–70 years were invited to participate in the screening program, with 17 980 individuals taking part in the trial. The experimental group showed a significant reduction in the detection rate of non-significant PCa (ISUP 1), cut by half (RR 0.46, 95% CI 0.33–0.64, p <0.001). The detection rate of ISUP ≥2 cancers was similar between trial arms (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.60–1.10) [ ]. A recent UK cohort study, ReIMAGINE, invited men aged 50–74 years to undergo MRI screening and PSA testing. Those with a positive MRI or elevated PSA density were recommended for the National Health Service PCa assessment. Among the 303 patients who completed the screening, 16% showed positive MRI findings. After the National Health Service referral, 9.6% of patients were diagnosed with clinically significant PCa compared to a 1% diagnosis of clinically insignificant PCa. Over half of the men with significant PCa on biopsies had a PSA level of 3 ng/mL (60%). This study could leverage targeted histological data from MRI-era cohorts to enhance current risk models, which are primarily based on transrectal ultrasound-guided biopsy data [ ]. While the recent significant results are standardizing the use of pre-biopsy MRI in PCa early detection pathways, the utilization of population-based PCa screening solely relying on MRI is not well-developed and, as a result, remains unestablished. Several factors such as the restricted accessibility, radiologists’ expertise dependence, elevated cost of multiparametric MRI, and the time-consuming nature of MRI limit its application. 6 PCa treatment trials When it comes to the treatment of patients diagnosed with PCa, a fundamental question arises: what is the evidence that radical treatment improves survival? Three pivotal trials have been undertaken to help inform our practice in this regard: the Scandinavian Prostate Cancer Group 4 (SPCG-4) [ , ], the Prostate Cancer Intervention versus Observation Trial (PIVOT) [ , ], and the Prostate Testing for Cancer and Treatment (ProtecT) trial [ , ] ( ). Among these trials, the SPCG-4 study stands out as the sole unequivocally positive trial, characterized by pre-dating the PSA screening era and predominantly enrolling patients with palpable disease during digital rectal exams. Together with the PIVOT, this trial was developed in an era when radical prostatectomies began with lymphadenectomy and if the frozen section was positive, the surgery was aborted (which might impact some outcomes). Together with the PIVOT, this trial was developed in an era when radical prostatectomies began with lymphadenectomy and if the frozen section was positive, the surgery was aborted (which might impact some outcomes). It should also be considered that mean PSA levels were elevated in these two trials (13 ng/mL in the SPCG-4 and 10 ng/mL in the PIVOT), potentially resulting in understaging compared to current protocols; consequently, the outcomes might be even better nowadays. On the flip side, contemporary treatments for advanced PCa provide enhanced survival, prompting the debate about whether the benefits seen in these trials would remain in the presence of superior therapeutic options after disease progression (docetaxel, cabazitaxel, new hormonal agents, etc. ). The PIVOT was similar to the SPCG-4, methodologically, and recruited a comparable population (45% low risk, 35% intermediate risk, and 20% high risk), yet 50% were diagnosed after PSA screening (compared to 12% in the SPCG-4), and radical prostatectomy did not significantly reduce PCa mortality or all-cause mortality compared with conservative management after 18.6 years of follow-up [ ]. This means that men with low-risk and low-PSA disease are good candidates for active surveillance, as is now the preferred care option for these men in urology guidelines [ ]. The ProtecT trial, the most contemporaneous trial, included a lower-risk cohort, with 75% diagnosed through PSA screening. Notably, patients were 77% low risk, 20% intermediate risk, 3% high risk, with a lower mean PSA value (5.8 ng/mL), and generally younger and healthier compared to the SPCG-4 and PIVOT cohorts [ , ]. In summary, these trials reveal a statistically significant advantage of radical prostatectomy over observation for the treatment of intermediate-risk PCa but without reaching clinical significance in the PIVOT and ProtecT trials. While the benefit for low-risk and high-risk patients remains more debatable concerning PCa mortality, the potential delay in metastasis development emerges as a clinically relevant outcome to include in shared decision-making with our patients. Future trials incorporating current management paradigms (multiparametric MRI, fusion biopsy, prostate-specific membrane antigen positron emission tomography, new antiandrogen therapies, etc. ) are needed to determine if active treatment truly prolongs survival in PCa patients diagnosed through PSA screening in the modern era. 7 PCa screening and society guidelines' position A summary of the main urological guidelines' recommendations is included in [ , , , , ]. A general consensus emphasizes the importance of not initiating PSA screening without prior discussion of its potential harms and benefits with men. The screening interval is established by considering PSA baseline levels and risk calculators, and is extended until a life expectancy of 10–15 years is reached. Early and more frequent PSA testing is recommended in cases with a high risk of PCa. Accepted high-risk factors include a family history of PCa, African descent, and BRCA2 mutations or other germline mutations. 8 The future: a risk-adapted strategy of combined factors Currently, there are multiple diagnostic tools available to assess the necessity of a biopsy, incorporating clinical data with PSA levels. They encompass demographic factors, race, family history, imaging (ultrasound and MRI), PSA, percent free PSA, prostate volume, PSA density, and the history of prior biopsies, among other considerations, including risk calculators and blood or urine biomarkers. While their use has been expanding in medical practice, it is important to note that risk calculators require calibration and consideration for differences in geographical populations [ ]. Early detection is recommended to lead to a significant reduction in mortality in screening programs. However, the NNI and NND, along with concerns about overdiagnosis and associated harms, highlight the need for improved accuracy in screening approaches before implementing them in the general population. Various strategies have been proposed in this regard. Retrospective observations on participants in, for example, the Malmo Preventive Project, a Swedish cardiovascular study conducted from 1974 to 1986, indicated that PSA levels at early ages (44–50 years) were a robust predictor of PCa up to 20 years later. Specifically, 81% of the PCa diagnosed at an advanced stage were found in men with early-baseline PSA levels above the age-specific median (>0.63 ng/mL) [ ]. These findings suggest the possibility of implementing a risk-adapted screening strategy, adjusting the frequency based on the early baseline PSA level. Furthermore, in this context, the recent Prostate Cancer Early Detection Study Based on a Baseline PSA Value in Young Men (PROBASE trial), a prospective randomized trial, compared immediate early PSA assessment at age 45 years versus deferred PSA evaluation at age 50 years in 46 642 participants. The first screening round results confirmed a low prevalence of PCa in the younger age group. Furthermore, it revealed an

with early-baseline PSA levels above the age-specific median (>0.63 ng/mL) [ ]. These findings suggest the possibility of implementing a risk-adapted screening strategy, adjusting the frequency based on the early baseline PSA level. Furthermore, in this context, the recent Prostate Cancer Early Detection Study Based on a Baseline PSA Value in Young Men (PROBASE trial), a prospective randomized trial, compared immediate early PSA assessment at age 45 years versus deferred PSA evaluation at age 50 years in 46 642 participants. The first screening round results confirmed a low prevalence of PCa in the younger age group. Furthermore, it revealed an even lower prevalence of unfavorable PCa and validated the expected PSA distribution across risk groups in alignment with prior studies: low risk (PSA <1.5 ng/mL: approximately 90%), intermediate risk (PSA 1.5–2.99 ng/mL: around 9%), and high risk (PSA >3 ng/mL: 1.5%) [ , ]. Other potential approaches for new screening methods include the utilization of multi-kallikrein panels or RNA-urine tests. The ProScreen study, a screening trial employing PSA followed by a 4-kallikrein panel and MRI, has recently conducted a feasibility evaluation in a sample of 400 men demonstrating proof-of-principle of a risk-stratified screening pathway and fewer men referred to a prostate biopsy using three screening tests (results pending from the ongoing large-scale trial) [ ]. In contrast, the ongoing BARCODE-1 trial, which has also recently published its feasibility evaluation, aims to assess a PCa screening program by selecting men based on their genetic risk of PCa using DNA extraction from saliva samples [ ]. In addition, population-based organized testing programs are currently being evaluated across 12 countries in the European Union within the PRAISE-U Consortium, to determine the implementation and cost-effectiveness of risk-stratified screening strategies [ ]. 9 Conclusion PCa screening has demonstrated a benefit in terms of reducing PCa mortality after 10 years of follow-up. Nevertheless, its application is not without risks, so a shared decision-making process must be ensured between the patient and the clinician before ordering the PSA test. Emerging tools such as MRI, genetic panels, and new biomarkers show promising opportunities to reduce these harms and the overdiagnosis of low-risk cancers. An individualized approach for each patient, based on detected risks and clinical parameters, helps guide different clinical pathways. Author contributions Study concept and design : Sigrid V. documents.title: Renal Cell Carcinoma

chunks.content: 1 Introduction Radical nephrectomy and inferior vena cava (IVC) thrombectomy provide reasonable long-term survival rates for patients with renal cancer and IVC thrombus [ , , ]. Surgical strategies included cavotomy, cavectomy, and partial IVC wall resection, according to the characteristics of the IVC thrombus [ , , , ]. Our team has reported a preoperative decision-making scheme for surgical strategies for cavectomy or thrombectomy based on factors such as the affected kidney side, establishment of collaterals, and IVC wall invasion [ ]. Among those factors, invasion of the IVC wall is the most important factor affecting surgical techniques for resection and cancer-specific survival [ , , ]. The involved IVC wall should be resected using cavectomy or partial IVC wall resection, depending on the extent of the lesion [ , , ]. However, techniques that can accurately predict preoperative IVC wall invasion are not well developed. In this study, a virtual vascular endoscopy was used to identify IVC wall invasion preoperatively. The accuracy of the technique and surgical and survival outcomes were also analysed. 2 Patients and methods 2.1 Patients A total of 36 patients with renal tumors and IVC thrombi who underwent CT and subsequent robot-assisted IVC thrombectomy (RA-IVCT) between June 2016 and March 2022 at the Chinese PLA General Hospital, Beijing, China were included. Virtual vascular endoscopy was performed to identify IVC invasion based on preoperative CT. All patients underwent multiparameter MRI within 1 week before surgery. If the IVC thrombus breaches the vessel wall and imaging reveals a loss of vessel wall delineation or heterogeneous enhancement of the wall, IVC wall invasion is presumed to be present [ , ]. This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Chinese PLA General Hospital (internal registration No. S2018-219-01). Written informed consent was obtained from all the patients. 2.2 Deep learning of virtual vascular endoscopy 2.2.1 Data requirements Virtual images were reconstructed using preoperative CT, and the parameters are shown in . 2.2.2 Main technology of virtual vascular endoscopy The core algorithm for virtual vascular endoscopy is illustrated in . During the reconstruction process, the Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine datasets were streamed into the deep learning models. The models then learn the import features for each organ based on previous datasets and evolve to achieve higher image accuracy. The middle datasets were subsequently used to produce a realistic image reconstruction, which can be viewed through digital virtual reality. The system architecture is described in the patent reference (Patent No.: US10713856B2). The renal tumor, thrombus, and IVC wall features were learned concentratedly. 2.2.3 Models for predicting IVC wall invasion Two major models are used for predicting IVC wall invasion. The first model focuses on image segmentation. This deep learning model learns the features of the kidney, renal tumor, IVC thrombus, and IVC wall by accurately labelling every pixel of the whole-body CT dataset for reconstruction. Invaded IVC wall has very similar imaging features to non-invaded IVC wall. Because there is a relatively small number of invaded pixels, higher accuracy is needed. The second classification model supplements the first and classifies each pixel individually, providing a positive or negative assessment. There are many features that affect whether the IVC is considered invasive, including the relationship between the tumor thrombus and IVC wall, the gray-value distribution in tumor thrombus segmentation images in the arterial and venous phases, the length and scope of the tumor thrombus, and whether the primary tumor has enveloped the IVC. By combining these features, the classification model can achieve a high degree of accuracy. As shown in , the imaging compares well with invasive vascular endoscopy and clearly highlights the location of the thrombus within the IVC wall. More importantly, the thrombus can be viewed in different directions, facilitating measurement of the thrombus length and location of IVC wall invasion in the axial, coronal, and sagittal planes and in the lateral decubitus or prone positions ( ). 2.3 Training of virtual vascular endoscopy Twenty patients with renal tumors with IVC thrombi who underwent high-resolution CT and subsequently underwent RA-IVCT were used to train the virtual vascular endoscopy (the training cohort). As illustrated in , cavectomy was used in patients with extensive IVC wall invasion. IVC thrombus specimens were serially sectioned, and pathological staining was performed to confirm the location of IVC wall invasion. The location of the invasion using sectioned specimens was compared with that of virtual vascular endoscopy predictions. Confirmation that the IVC was free of invasion enabled the calibration of the model during RA-IVCT. Using this methodology, the confidence in the accuracy of the model can be increased. 2.4 Evaluation of the predictive accuracy of virtual vascular endoscopy After satisfactory calibration of the model, 16 patients who underwent RA-IVCT also underwent preoperative virtual vascular endoscopy to predict IVC wall invasion. The accuracy of

The location of the invasion using sectioned specimens was compared with that of virtual vascular endoscopy predictions. Confirmation that the IVC was free of invasion enabled the calibration of the model during RA-IVCT. Using this methodology, the confidence in the accuracy of the model can be increased. 2.4 Evaluation of the predictive accuracy of virtual vascular endoscopy After satisfactory calibration of the model, 16 patients who underwent RA-IVCT also underwent preoperative virtual vascular endoscopy to predict IVC wall invasion. The accuracy of preoperative virtual vascular endoscopy was determined using intraoperative serial sectioning and pathological staining (the validation cohort). As illustrated in , the cavectomy technique was applied in patients with good collateral circulation and multiple sites of IVC wall invasion. Suspected IVC wall invasion detected by virtual vascular endoscopy and macroscopic examination was marked with sutures and finally confirmed using the whole-mount technique by two senior pathologists. The accuracy of the virtual vascular endoscopy model can be further evaluated using this method. 2.5 Virtual vascular endoscopy for locating IVC wall invasion In patients with limited IVC wall invasion but without collateral establishment, cavotomy, thrombus removal, and IVC reconstruction were performed ( ). In patients with invasion of the posterior wall of the IVC and a soft texture of the thrombus, the cavotomy technique was applied, and IVC wall invasion was confirmed visually via RA-IVCT ( ). However, in cases of invasion of the anterior wall of the IVC and confirmed infiltration into the IVC wall, partial IVC wall resection was performed ( ). Supplementary video related to this article can be found at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajur.2024.08.004 The following are the supplementary data related to this article: Supplemental Video 1 An introduction of virtual vascular endoscopy. Multimedia component 2 2.6 Surgical approach The surgical strategies followed our previously published studies, including the necessity of angioembolization of the renal artery, position changing, liver mobilization, liver hilum vessels clamping, and veno-venous or cardiopulmonary bypass, which depend on the level of venous tumor thrombus [ , , , , , ]. 2.7 Data analysis Continuous variables are presented as medians and ranges and were analysed using a t -test or ANOVA after estimating the variance between groups. Categorical variables are presented as frequencies and percentages and were analysed using the Chi-square test. All the statistical analyses were performed using PASW Statistics software (version 18.0; IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). A p -value of <0.05 was considered to indicate statistical signiﬁcance. The datasets used and analysed during the current study are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request. 3 Results The baseline patient characteristics are shown in . The median tumor size and length of the extended IVC tumor thrombi in the training and validation cohorts were 9.0 cm versus 9.3 cm and 6.8 cm versus 4.8 cm, respectively. Eleven of the 13 patients with IVC thrombus in the training cohort and five of the nine patients in the validation cohort with IVC wall invasion underwent RA-IVCT via the cavectomy technique. Six patients in the training cohort and four in the validation cohort received preoperative targeted therapy. In the validation cohort, eight of the nine patients with IVC wall invasion were accurately predicted using virtual vascular endoscopy. One patient who received preoperative targeted therapy with IVC wall invasion could not be accurately assessed using this new technique. Six patients without IVC wall invasion were accurately identified. There was a false-positive case in which intensive IVC wall adhesion was observed instead of IVC invasion by the tumor thrombus. The patient received preoperative targeted therapy. Thirteen patients in the validation cohort were accurately evaluated according to preoperative MRI by two experienced radiologists independently. The diagnostic consistency of MRI and virtual vascular endoscopy was fine (Kappa value was 0.613, ). We performed a subgroup analysis of patients with level I-II IVC thrombi ( ) and compared the surgical outcomes between the training and validation cohorts in the subgroup. The training and validation cohorts comprised 12 and 13 patients, respectively. Of these, four cases in the training cohort and one case in the validation cohort involved left-sided renal tumors with IVC thrombi. In the training cohort, six of the eight patients with IVC wall invasion underwent cavectomy, while three of the seven patients with IVC wall invasion underwent cavectomy in the validation cohort. Two patients in the training cohort and four in the validation cohort underwent partial IVC wall resection. The median operation time and estimated blood loss volume were lower in the validation cohort than in the training cohort (194 min vs. 309 min, p =0.007; 400 mL vs. 1150 mL, p <0.001). The longer operation time in the training cohort may be primarily due to the inclusion of more left-sided

In the training cohort, six of the eight patients with IVC wall invasion underwent cavectomy, while three of the seven patients with IVC wall invasion underwent cavectomy in the validation cohort. Two patients in the training cohort and four in the validation cohort underwent partial IVC wall resection. The median operation time and estimated blood loss volume were lower in the validation cohort than in the training cohort (194 min vs. 309 min, p =0.007; 400 mL vs. 1150 mL, p <0.001). The longer operation time in the training cohort may be primarily due to the inclusion of more left-sided patients who required repositioning. The validation cohort had fewer complications than did the training cohort ( ). In the training cohort, two patients who underwent cavectomy presented with lower extremities edema. One patient experienced perioperative mortality due to cardiac arrest, which resulted from pre-existing coronary heart disease. There was one case of lymph node metastasis and two cases of distant metastasis in the training cohort, whereas there were two cases of lymph node metastasis and three cases of distant metastasis in the validation cohort. Adjuvant targeted therapy was prescribed to six patients in the training cohort and three patients in the validation cohort with IVC wall invasion or metastasis. The median follow-up for all the patients was 31.8 (range 8.0–75.0) months. Among the nine patients who underwent cavectomy in the two groups with level I-II IVC thrombus, five patients developed new-onset metastasis postoperatively, resulting in three deaths. For the six patients who underwent partial IVC resection, new-onset metastasis occurred in three patients postoperatively, resulting in two deaths. 4 Discussion In this study, we developed a virtual vascular endoscope to identify IVC wall invasion and assist in surgical strategy planning. The results of this study showed that this new technique offers good accuracy in predicting IVC wall invasion and can guide surgeons in deciding between partial and segmental IVC resection during RA-IVCT. However, certain factors, such as preoperative targeted therapy, influence the accuracy of this technique. Patients with tumor infiltration into the IVC wall are indicated for partial IVC resection or cavectomy [ , , ] because IVC wall invasion is an independent poor prognostic factor for both overall survival and cancer-specific survival [ , , , , ]. Renal tumors with a tumor thrombus invading the IVC wall are classified as pT3c according to the tumor-node-metastasis staging system, regardless of the level of thrombus [ ]. Studies have shown that IVC wall invasion is associated with poor overall survival and progression-free survival [ ], and complete tumor resection and negative vascular margins maximize the survival benefit in these patients [ ]. Therefore, segmental or partial IVC resection is required for patients with IVC wall invasion. Nevertheless, in patients without well-established collaterals, cavectomy in acute situations may cause hypotension resulting from reduced venous return, postoperative renal insufficiency, lower extremity edema, or abdominal wall varicosity [ , ]. A study on acute IVC ligation showed a 9% mortality rate, and postoperative lower extremity swelling occurred in more than one-third of the patients [ ]. In our previous study, seven of 30 patients developed mild transient lower extremity edema [ ]. One patient died of cardiac arrest due to pre-existing coronary heart disease [ ]. In this study, we found that lower extremity edema and perioperative death were more frequent in patients who underwent segmental IVC resection than in those who underwent partial IVC wall resection. Thus, partial IVC resection is recommended for patients with limited IVC wall invasion if the collateral system is not well established, which could be associated with fewer complications. It is important to assess the location and extent of IVC wall invasion preoperatively. In 1991, Fujimoto et al. [ ] performed an angioscopy to observe IVC thrombi and direct invasion of the IVC wall. A fiberscope was directed to the area of interest in the IVC via a transfemoral 5-Fr catheter. Saline was infused to enable angioscopic observation of the IVC wall. Patients with IVC invasion underwent cavectomy [ ]. However, certain disadvantages limit its use. First, it is invasive and increases the risk of thrombus shedding. Second, this technique is not feasible for patients with complete IVC obstruction. Subsequently, Loh-Doyle et al. [ ] applied vena cavoscopy and used a flexible cystoscope to detect residual and intraluminal tumor involvement intraoperatively. However, this technique cannot be used for surgical planning. High-quality diagnostic imaging techniques are the cornerstone of preoperative planning and management. Among them, MRI plays a key role in detecting IVC wall invasion. A series of studies have shown that preoperative MRI could predict IVC wall invasion with a positive predictive value of 75%–92% [ , , ]. Moreover, preoperative cine MRI and radiomics models based on MRI also show high accuracy in predicting IVC wall invasion

obstruction. Subsequently, Loh-Doyle et al. [ ] applied vena cavoscopy and used a flexible cystoscope to detect residual and intraluminal tumor involvement intraoperatively. However, this technique cannot be used for surgical planning. High-quality diagnostic imaging techniques are the cornerstone of preoperative planning and management. Among them, MRI plays a key role in detecting IVC wall invasion. A series of studies have shown that preoperative MRI could predict IVC wall invasion with a positive predictive value of 75%–92% [ , , ]. Moreover, preoperative cine MRI and radiomics models based on MRI also show high accuracy in predicting IVC wall invasion [ , ]. Our team used contrast-enhanced ultrasonography to detect IVC wall invasion preoperatively and intraoperatively. The model has a satisfactory predictive value [ ]. However, all of these methods involve two-dimensional imaging and require professional guidance from a radiologist. Recently, three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction and virtual reality technologies based on preoperative imaging have been applied to facilitate surgical planning and intraoperative navigation. Porpiglia et al. [ ] introduced their experience using a 3D elastic augmented reality system to identify the location of capsular involvement in prostate cancer during the nerve-sparing phase of robot-assisted radical prostatectomy. Grosso et al. [ ] introduced the use of 3D virtual models to guide preoperative planning in partial nephrectomy. Schiavina et al. [ ] applied real-time augmented reality models to guide nerve sparing during robot-assisted radical prostatectomy in surgical planning. In addition to guiding the surgical strategies, 3D virtual models also have advantages in terms of surgical outcomes and functional preservation. A comparative analysis has confirmed that the use of 3D virtual models could improve the oncologic and functional outcomes following robot-assisted partial nephrectomy [ ]. Virtual vascular endoscopy combines the advantages of endoscopy and virtual reality technology to successfully identify IVC wall invasion, enabling surgeons to perform more accurate surgical planning. The initial data showed that this technique accurately examined and located IVC wall invasion. This artificial intelligence technology and virtual reality capability can quickly process data and thus speed up diagnosis. Moreover, less professional guidance is required from radiologists. Thus, virtual vascular endoscopy could be incorporated into robotic imaging systems in the future. Using fixed data points, laser sensors can collect data, enabling the system to perform virtual vascular endoscopy in real time. We found that preoperative targeted therapy may affect the prediction of IVC wall invasion by influencing CT parameters and pathological changes. In the present study, the predictive value of virtual vascular endoscopy did not correlate with the postoperative pathological results in two patients. Antiangiogenic agents used in vascular endothelial growth factor-targeted therapy induce objective changes in renal cell carcinoma, including decreased attenuation and increased tumor necrosis [ ]. Reduced radiological enhancement may increase the difficulty of identifying between the tumor thrombus and the IVC wall. However, long-term targeted therapy may promote adhesion and fibrotic processes in vascular walls. Harshman et al. [ ] reported that presurgical targeted therapy was associated with an increased incidence and grade of intraoperative adhesions. However, further investigations with larger sample sizes are needed to verify the impact of preoperative targeted therapy on the diagnosis of lesions by imaging and pathology. 5 Conclusion Virtual vascular endoscopy is a new technique for the preoperative identification of IVC wall invasion. According to the extent of IVC wall invasion and the collateral situation, surgeons decide whether to perform partial or segmental IVC resection during RA-IVCT. However, certain clinical factors can affect the accuracy of this technique. Therefore, studies with larger sample sizes are required for a better understanding and improvement of this new technique. documents.title: Bladder Cancer Non-Muscle Invasive

chunks.content: 1 Introduction Bladder cancer (BC) is the 7th most commonly diagnosed cancer in males, whilst it drops to the 10th position when both genders are considered [ ]. In non-metastatic BC, approximately 75% of patients present with disease confined to the mucosa (pTa, carcinoma in situ [CIS]) or submucosa (pT1), but most of the cancer-specific mortality is associated with pT2–T4 tumors [ ]. The current treatment of clinically non-metastatic muscle-invasive BC (MIBC) is associated with significant morbidity and mortality [ , ]. Since it generally affects elderly people with more comorbidities, postoperative complications are more likely to occur [ ]. MIBC only reaches a 50% 5-year survival rate [ , ], despite aggressive treatment with radical cystectomy (RC) and pelvic lymph node dissection, currently being the gold-standard approach [ , , , , , , ]. RC is related to infectious, genitourinary, gastrointestinal, and wound-related complications, occurring in up to 58% and perisurgical mortality up to 4.7% (at 90 days) of patients with MIBC [ ]. Additionally, sexual function and social and/or economic aspects have a significant impact on quality of life (QoL) [ , ]. All of these complications reflect the need for bladder-sparing options for non-metastatic MIBC [ ]. Several bladder-sparing therapies have been described, including chemotherapy (CMT), radiotherapy (RT), and trimodality therapy (TMT) [ ]. RT alone has been shown to have worse outcomes when compared to chemoradiotherapy and TMT [ , ]. On the other hand, CMT has shown a limited role as a single or dual therapy compared to TMT [ ]. While all monotherapies are less effective than RC and are not recommended as curative therapy [ , , ], TMT has shown favorable results. In fact, TMT, which consists of maximal transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT) followed by RT with concurrent radiosensitizing CMT, is currently the most common bladder preservation strategy [ ]. Immunotherapy (IMT) agents such as immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have provided new perspectives in the treatment of MIBC during the last years [ ]. Among them, inhibitors of programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1), programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1), and cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated antigen 4 (CTLA-4) are currently available therapies with different results and indications [ ]. Among the limitations of bladder-sparing strategies, the evidence is still limited and heterogeneous in the population and inclusion criteria. Additionally, cohorts are small and do not have long-term follow-up, and there are no prospective randomized studies comparing outcomes between RC and TMT. Reviews and meta-analyses published to date provide discordant results that preclude drawing concrete conclusions about therapies [ , , ]. In addition, IMT is a developing alternative for which few published results exist and have not yet been included in reviews as a therapy alone [ ]. The aim of this study was to systematically analyze the most recent scientific literature regarding organ preservation strategies in the treatment of non-metastatic MIBC, comparing oncologic and functional outcomes, and QoL between RC and TMT, in addition to results of novel IMT agents for BC. Additionally, a meta-analysis was performed to compare the 5-year overall survival (OS) outcomes between both treatments across multiple studies, enhancing the quality of the conclusions. 2 Acquisition of evidence and analyses The literature search was conducted using PubMed (access date: August 27, 2023), Google Scholar (access date: September 3, 2023), EMBASE (access date: September 11, 2023), Wiley Library (access date: September 11, 2023), and ClinicalTrials.gov (access date: October 19, 2023). The reporting of this systematic review was guided by the standards of the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement [ ]. The protocol was registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO), in accordance with PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO registration ID 574880). The search was performed by two independent reviewers using the keywords: “Radical cystectomy”, “Bladder-sparing”, “Bladder cancer”, “Bladder preservation”, “Muscle-invasive bladder cancer” or “MIBC”, “Trimodal therapy”, “Immunotherapy”, and “Chemoradiation”. We included original articles, retrospective studies, prospective studies, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, congress abstracts (meeting-driven poster or oral communication), and clinical trials between January 2012 and December 2024 involving RC, TMT, and IMT. Only articles in English were included; however, the search was not limited by language. We excluded letters, editorials, case reports, prevalence studies, study protocols, narrative reviews or qualitative studies, pre-clinical studies (non-human animal models or in vitro studies), and non-peer-reviewed articles except clinical guidelines. In addition, we excluded articles that were duplicated on different platforms or with full texts that were unable to be accessed. Finally, publications that showed unsuitable participant criteria (patients without diagnosis of MIBC or CIS, and without chemoradiotherapy, RC, TMT, or IMT [alone or concurrent]), unsuitable technical or clinical outcomes (no report of prognosis, progression, or survival), and unsuitable outcome-report format (no OS or survival curves, disease-specific survival, disease-free survival [DFS], salvage cystectomy [SC] reported at 3 years,

study protocols, narrative reviews or qualitative studies, pre-clinical studies (non-human animal models or in vitro studies), and non-peer-reviewed articles except clinical guidelines. In addition, we excluded articles that were duplicated on different platforms or with full texts that were unable to be accessed. Finally, publications that showed unsuitable participant criteria (patients without diagnosis of MIBC or CIS, and without chemoradiotherapy, RC, TMT, or IMT [alone or concurrent]), unsuitable technical or clinical outcomes (no report of prognosis, progression, or survival), and unsuitable outcome-report format (no OS or survival curves, disease-specific survival, disease-free survival [DFS], salvage cystectomy [SC] reported at 3 years, 5 years, 10 years, or 15 years) were excluded. After a first phase of evidence screening based on the evaluation of titles and abstracts, 107 articles were selected for independent evaluation of their full texts by the reviewers. When there were disagreements on inclusion, these were resolved by a third reviewer. According to the inclusion and exclusion criteria, 21 articles were included. The results and syntheses of each study are described in , , , and in the main text (narrative). This systematic review process is described in the PRISMA flow chart ( ). For the bias risk evaluation of the studies, the Risk of Bias 2 and the Risk Of Bias in Non-randomized Studies-of Exposure (ROBINS-E) tools for randomized and non-randomized studies according to Cochrane Collaboration were used to assess the bias risk classification of the studies [ , , ]. The evaluation criteria domains included randomization process or selection of participants, deviations from intended interventions or confounding factors, missing outcome data, measurement of the outcome or exposure, and selection of the reported results. The studies were classified as “high-bias risk”, “low-bias risk”, and “unclear-bias risk”, or “some bias risk concerns” based on the above criteria. For quality evaluation of the studies included, the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) standard in the Cochrane Collaboration was used for quality classification [ ]. The evaluation criteria domains included risk of bias, imprecision, inconsistency, indirectness, and publication bias, in addition to effect, dose response, and residual confounding. A study with a score of “4 plus” was considered high quality, “3 plus” moderate quality, “2 plus” low quality, and “1 plus” very low quality based on the above criteria. It should be noted that since completed randomized clinical trials on this topic are scarce, none of the studies achieved the maximum score of 4 plus. For the evaluation and comparison of the target clinical outcome, a meta-analysis including only studies that compared TMT and RC was performed. GraphPad Prism v10.2.3 (GraphPad Software, Boston, MA, USA) and MedCalc Statistical Software version 19.2.6 (MedCalc Software bv, Ostend, Belgium) were adopted for the figure drawing and statistical analysis, respectively. Proportions, odds ratios, and 95% confidence intervals were used to evaluate and compare the survival rates or OS outcomes at 5 years between TMT (intervention) and RC (control). A random-effects model was used for the meta-analysis [ ]. 3 Synthesis of evidence After the search, evidence was collected from 21 articles that included a total of 47 647 patients. Summarized information for each of them can be found in , , , . Once the selection and analysis of articles were done, the risk of bias and quality assessment were performed using the Risk of Bias 2 tool, ROBINS-E tool, and GRADE classification for 15 of the 21 articles as shown in , , and . The remaining six articles were excluded from the analysis since they were partial result reports from clinical trials, but were discussed in the review. Overall, the risk of bias analysis showed higher risk for the “randomization process or selection of patients” and “selection of reported results” domains, but lower risk for the “missing outcome data” and “measurement of the outcome or exposure” domains ( ). Regarding the quality analysis, 53% of the articles were classified as “low quality” and 47% as “moderate quality” ( and ). 3.1 TMT Currently, the gold standard for treating MIBC is RC with bilateral pelvic lymphadenectomy and urinary diversion. This involves removal of the bladder and its surrounding tissues, with an extended surgical time and hospital stay length, and patients requiring 3 months to 6 months to recover to baseline levels [ , ]. Nowadays, cisplatin-based neoadjuvant CMT (NAC) is a therapeutic strategy used prior to primary cystectomy in MIBC with methotrexate, vinblastine, doxorubicin and cisplatin (MVAC), gemcitabine and cisplatin, and dose-dense MVAC [ ]. The reason for NAC is to treat micrometastatic disease at the time of diagnosis, when the burden of disease is the lowest [ ]. Adjuvant therapy, according to American and European guidelines, lacks quality evidence to support its impact on survival to date [ ]. Despite being the main treatment, RC only provides about a 49% 5-year survival

to 6 months to recover to baseline levels [ , ]. Nowadays, cisplatin-based neoadjuvant CMT (NAC) is a therapeutic strategy used prior to primary cystectomy in MIBC with methotrexate, vinblastine, doxorubicin and cisplatin (MVAC), gemcitabine and cisplatin, and dose-dense MVAC [ ]. The reason for NAC is to treat micrometastatic disease at the time of diagnosis, when the burden of disease is the lowest [ ]. Adjuvant therapy, according to American and European guidelines, lacks quality evidence to support its impact on survival to date [ ]. Despite being the main treatment, RC only provides about a 49% 5-year survival [ ] ( ). Regarding QoL after RC assessed by SF-36 and QLC-C30 questionnaires, most of the patients showed poor urinary and sexual function along with impaired body image and emotional status [ ]. Furthermore, even patients suitable for RC often choose to postpone this option [ ]. Currently, TMT is the most established bladder preservation strategy in non-metastatic MIBC [ ]. TMT protocols vary among clinical trials and regions, but they broadly consist of maximal TURBT followed by RT with concurrent radiosensitizing CMT [ ]. In case of muscle-invasive residual disease at restaging, SC should be performed [ , , ]. Patient suitability for TMT is crucial for successful oncological management. The main selection criteria are unifocal tumors <6 cm suitable for complete macroscopic resection, cT2–cT3a tumors, absence of extensive CIS, no bilateral hydronephrosis, and good bladder function [ ]. The most relevant results of TMT to date are summarized in . Giacalone et al. [ ] retrospectively analyzed 475 patients undergoing TMT. OS rates at 5 years, 10 years, and 15 years were 57%, 39%, and 25%, respectively, being better for cT2 (65%, 46%, and 29%, respectively) than for cT3 (42%, 26%, and 17%, respectively). SC requirement rates at 5 years and 10 years were 29% and 31%, respectively. Six deaths occurred due to treatment and one patient required cystectomy for treatment-related toxicity [ ]. Softness et al. [ ] included 2048 patients with cT2–cT3 cN0 cM0 MIBC in their retrospective analysis, where 1812 were treated with RC and 236 with TMT. In their study, 5-year OS rates for RC and TMT were 53% and 44%, while 10-year OS rates were 40% and 33%, respectively. However, patients treated with RC were significantly younger (64 years vs. 70 years, p <0.01) and had a lower Charlson comorbidity index than patients treated with TMT. Furthermore, RC patients were more likely to be treated in academic centers. Interestingly, when sensitivity analyses were applied to reduce confounding factors by restricting the cohort to patients between 40 years and 70 years and Charlson comorbidity index of 0 points (1104 patients undergoing RC and 166 undergoing TMT), they found a higher 5-year OS rate for TMT compared to RC, without reaching statistical significance (65% vs. 57%, respectively; p =0.35) [ ]. Selection criteria for TMT have recently been updated by Zlotta et al. [ ] in a multicenter retrospective analysis including 722 patients with MIBC, with solitary tumors <7 cm, clinical stage T2–T4 N0 M0, no or unilateral hydronephrosis, no CIS, and no multifocal tumors; 440 patients underwent RC and 282 TMT. Notably, unlike other studies, all patients had similar inclusion criteria, being all suitable for both therapies. Similar rates were observed for 5-year metastasis-free survival (74% for RC and 75% for TMT; p =0.95). Additionally, 5-year cancer-specific survival was 80% for RC and 82% for TMT ( p =0.25), and 5-year DFS was 75% for RC and 73% for TMT ( p =0.93). Remarkably, 5-year OS was significantly higher for TMT compared to RC (73% vs . 66%, respectively; p =0.01). In fact, only 38 (13%) TMT patients underwent SC, of which 37 (97%) presented muscle-invasive recurrence and there was only one (3%) treatment-related toxicity. The 5-year cancer-specific survival of patients undergoing SC was equivalent to those treated with TMT without the need for SC (85% vs. 84%) [ ]. So far, this is the only study comparing RC with TMT in patients with updated and similar inclusion criteria, suitable for both therapies, which reinforces the evidence that both therapies have similar oncological outcomes when using broad inclusion criteria [ ]. A meta-analysis was performed with only studies that compared the 5-year survival rates of TMT and RC which included a total of 29 308 patients. A forest plot analysis showed a high heterogeneity among studies (Cochran's Q =65.80 [ p <0.001]; I 2 =93.92%), and no significant differences between TMT and RC (random effects; p =0.4) as shown in . Concerning QoL, one Markov model simulation study compared TMT versus RC by measuring quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) and reported a gain of 0.59 QALYs with TMT when compared to RC (7.83 vs. 7.24, respectively) [ ]. A forest plot analysis showed a high heterogeneity among studies (Cochran's Q =65.80 [ p <0.001]; I 2 =93.92%), and no significant differences between TMT and RC (random effects; p =0.4) as shown in . Concerning QoL, one Markov model simulation study compared TMT versus RC by measuring quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) and reported a gain of 0.59 QALYs with TMT when compared to RC (7.83 vs. 7.24, respectively) [ ]. Mak et al. [ ] performed a cross-sectional bi-institutional study that compared the long-term QoL in MIBC patients treated with TMT versus RC. Patients with non-metastatic cT2–cT4 MIBC, suitable for RC and disease free for 2 years, were included in the study; 64 patients who received TMT and 109 patients who underwent RC answered the questionnaires 9 years and 7 years after the procedure, respectively. The results showed that both TMT and RC patients had acceptable long-term QoL, but TMT patients were associated with improved general aspects (high physical state score, role, social, emotional, and cognitive functioning, with less fatigue, pain, nausea, and vomiting), urinary (bowel function), and sexual (sexual function and body image) compared to RC ones [ ]. Their study supported that TMT could be a good alternative to RC for suitable patients regarding QoL. In addition, Kool et al. [ ] compared cost-effectiveness between RC and TMT using Markov model simulation, observing that life-years gained at 5 years and 10 years were slightly higher for TMT when compared to RC, with 4.1 years vs. 4 years and 6.53 life-years vs . 6.40 life-years at 5 years and 10 years, respectively. Additionally, the study analyzed QALYs at 5 years and 10 years, observing moderately higher values for TMT when compared to RC (3.63 vs. 3.35 after 5 years and 5.68 vs. 5.33 after 10 years, respectively) [ ]. Regarding costs, despite being similar at 5 years, they differed at 10 years (33 286 USD vs. 40 197 USD) [ ]. Meanwhile, Magee et al. [ ] reported median costs for RC and TMT of 30 577 USD and 18 979 USD, respectively, being significantly higher for RC ( p <0.001). However, the cost associated with follow-up and care was higher for TMT than RC (3094 USD/year vs. 1974 USD/year, respectively) with a non-significant difference ( p =0.09) [ ]. Finally, Huddart et al. [ ] compared several outcomes of patients undergoing TMT versus RC in the Selective Bladder Preservation Against Radical Excision feasibility study, finding that patients undergoing TMT showed an improvement in mean global health status and social functioning, while they were reduced in the RC group [ ]. 3.2 New treatments using IMT associated with other therapies IMT, such as ICIs, has provided new perspectives in the treatment of MIBC [ ]. Current indications include TURBT and ICIs as single or combined agents, as well as standard NAC [ ]. These treatment options may improve the efficacy of standard CMT and become options for cisplatin-ineligible patients [ , ]. Among bladder-sparing therapies, IMT combined with chemoradiotherapy, RT, or CMT has been assessed. These bladder-sparing therapies involving IMT are associated with TURBT, where PD-1 inhibitors such as tislelizumab or pembrolizumab, in addition to PD-L1 inhibitors such as atezolizumab and CTLA-4 inhibitors such as ipilimumab, have been the most used [ ]. PD-1, PD-L1, and CTLA-4 are key proteins involved in the regulation of the immune response against tumors [ , ]. These molecules have specific mechanisms that enhance or inhibit T-cell function and their interaction with tumor cells in the tumor microenvironment [ ]. In IMT, antibodies serve as inhibitors of these proteins, blocking their inhibitory signals, allowing T-cell activation, and therefore improving the ability of the immune system [ , ]. The most relevant results of IMT to date are summarized in . Hu et al. [ ] retrospectively evaluated neoadjuvant therapy in patients undergoing RC, comparing IMT, CMT, and immunochemotherapy in patients with MIBC. Although this was not a bladder preservation trial, it did have a subgroup of patients eventually not undergoing RC. In fact, 33 patients declined RC; therefore, TURBT was performed. Of them, 10 patients received immunochemotherapy, 15 CMT, and eight IMT. After a median follow-up of 13 months, 31 (93.94%) achieved DFS while two patients treated with immunochemotherapy and CMT did not achieve DFS [ ]. In another series, Xu et al. [ ] retrospectively analyzed 25 patients with MIBC unable to undergo or refusing RC. They were treated with TURBT and IMT, specifically tislelizumab (19 patients) or toripalimab (six patients) in combination with RT or CMT. They were treated with TURBT and IMT, specifically tislelizumab (19 patients) or toripalimab (six patients) in combination with RT or CMT. For patients treated with tislelizumab, the 1-year OS and DFS were 100% and 94.7%, respectively, while for patients treated with toripalimab, both were 83.3%. Additionally, the authors mentioned that PD-L1 expression and CMT had no impact on outcomes [ ]. One of the limitations of this study was that, although the number of patients who received each drug was reported, the treatment combination that each patient received was not specified. Dahl et al. [ ] reported the long-term survival and toxicity results of the NRG Oncology RTOG 0524 study. Their prospective study enrolled 65 patients divided into two groups treated with daily radiation and weekly CMT (paclitaxel) with or without IMT (trastuzumab), respectively. Despite a lower 5-year OS within the IMT group versus the non-IMT group (25% vs. 37.8%, respectively), the 5-year DFS was higher for IMT patients compared to non-IMT patients (15% vs. 31.1%, respectively). There were 18 deaths in the IMT group and 33 in the non-IMT group, of which 11 and 16 were due to disease, respectively [ ]. A promising study of IMT with durvalumab with or without RT in older patients with lymph node metastatic disease not undergoing complete TURBT has recently been reported by Joshi et al. [ ]. Results showed a complete response of 50%, a 1-year PFS of 73%, and 1-year and 2-year OS of 83.8% and 76.8%, respectively [ ]. Several clinical trials evaluating IMT in this clinical scenario are currently underway, showing only initial results so far ( ). One phase 2 trial, combining pembrolizumab with gemcitabine and RT in patients refusing or not being eligible for RC, estimated a 1-year DFS rate of 77% and complete response rates of 83% to 100% [ ]. Another phase 2 study including 27 patients treated with pembrolizumab together with chemoradiation reported a complete response rate of 88%, a 2-year metastasis-free survival rate of 78%, and a freedom from locoregional progression rate of 87%, with a median survival of 39 months [ ]. Vazquez-Estevez et al. [ ] evaluated atezolizumab plus RT in 14 patients and observed a 100% complete response rate [ ]. Another phase 2 trial with durvalumab plus tremelimumab combined with RT in 32 patients showed an 81% complete response with 6-month DFS and OS rates of 76% and 93%, respectively, and only two patients who went to salvage RC due to MIBC recurrence [ ]. Meanwhile, the combination of nivolumab and RT showed a complete response in six out of 14 patients [ ]. Finally, another study using tislelizumab associated with NAC (paclitaxel) in 22 patients showed a complete response in 13 of them and a partial response in nine [ ]. Until the date of this review, there are no published studies comparing the efficacy among available ICIs. 4 Discussion To address the knowledge gap in bladder-sparing therapies for non-metastatic MIBC, it is essential to possess up-to-date information for informed treatment decision-making. This review offers a comprehensive knowledge base on this subject, identifying best practices, evaluating the effectiveness of various therapeutic approaches, and guiding treatment strategies to meet the specific needs of each patient. RC remains the gold standard treatment and the most studied to date [ , , , , ]. However, it is related to elevated morbidity, with a large segment of patients not being able to undergo the surgery, reflecting the need for alternatives such as TMT and IMT [ , , , , ]. However, it is difficult to compare all the selected studies with each other, since there are key differences in their design: different clinical variables and demographic characteristics, mixed inclusion criteria, various outcome measurement methodologies, variability in healthcare center levels, and staff expertise, among others. In this study, a meta-analysis was performed to assess the survival of patients undergoing RC compared to TMT. Only five articles were included in this section as they were the only ones containing data that allowed statistical measurement of both strategies. For the meta-analysis, a random-effects analysis was chosen over a fixed-effect analysis for three reasons: a) a high expectation of heterogeneity among the study results as there are main differences in terms of setting, design, populations, and patient selection, b) broader generalizability of the effects as selected studies show a sample of a larger population of studies and, c) the potential variability in true effect sizes
